Content:
We've seen how to approximate definite integrals using a graphing calculator. In this lesson, we'll apply the techniques we've learned to approximate improper integrals.

Content:
Suppose we wish to evaluate the following improper integral to three decimal places:

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x]

Content:
Your graphing calculator is unlikely to include an [MATH: \infty] button, so we cannot directly enter this improper integral into our graphing calculator.

Content:
However, recall that, by definition
[MATH: \int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x = \lim\limits_{a\to\infty} \int_1^a \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
So instead, let's consider the definite integral

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^a \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
We now use our graphing calculator to approximate the above integral for increasing values of [MATH: a{:}]

Content:
- Setting [MATH: a=9,] we have
[MATH: \int_1^9 \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.170]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
- Setting [MATH: a=99,] we have
[MATH: \int_1^{99} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
- Setting [MATH: a=999,] we have
[MATH: \int_1^{999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
Since the integrals with upper limits [MATH: 99] and [MATH: 999] both give [MATH: 0.171] to [MATH: 3] decimal places, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

items.title: Some Important Notes

sections.normalized_html: Before we look at another example, you should note the following important points:
sections.readable_text: Before we look at another example, you should note the following important points:

sections.normalized_html:
• In the previous example, you may wonder why we didn't approximate our improper integral by picking a very large value for [MATH: a] right off the bat, e.g., [MATH: \int_1^{999\,999\,999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x.] If we were to try this, one of two things might happen:

    • The first is that the calculator might report an error. This is likely due to a lack of physical memory available.

    • The second is that the calculator might give an incorrect answer! Evaluating the above on a TI-84 Plus CE-T gives [MATH: \int_1^{999\,999\,999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 1.348\times 10^{-19}] which is incorrect! Again, this incorrect answer is likely due to physical limitations that apply to all calculators.

    The critical takeaway is that the only safe way to approximate improper integrals is by using the method described earlier.

  • In the last example, we increased the upper limit by appending an extra digit [MATH: 9] each time. [MATH: \int_1^9\qquad \int_1^{99}, \qquad \int_1^{999}, \qquad \int_1^{9\,999}, \qquad \ldots] If your calculator reports errors before you've reached a definite answer, consider increasing the upper limit more slowly. For example, [MATH: \int_1^{10}\qquad \int_1^{100}, \qquad \int_1^{200}, \qquad \int_1^{300}, \qquad \ldots\,.]

  • Also, bear in mind that some integrals will converge faster than others. Integrals that converge slowly may require us to pick large values for [MATH: a] before we can be sure of our final answer.

  • Finally, throughout this lesson, you may assume that all improper integrals we'll encounter are convergent and that all of the functions we'll integrate decay to zero "rapidly enough" for this method to be suitable.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We've seen how to approximate definite integrals using a graphing calculator. In this lesson, we'll apply the techniques we've learned to approximate improper integrals.

Content:
Suppose we wish to evaluate the following improper integral to three decimal places:

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x]

Content:
Your graphing calculator is unlikely to include an [MATH: \infty] button, so we cannot directly enter this improper integral into our graphing calculator.

Content:
However, recall that, by definition
[MATH: \int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x = \lim\limits_{a\to\infty} \int_1^a \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
So instead, let's consider the definite integral

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^a \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
We now use our graphing calculator to approximate the above integral for increasing values of [MATH: a{:}]

Content:
- Setting [MATH: a=9,] we have
[MATH: \int_1^9 \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.170]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
- Setting [MATH: a=99,] we have
[MATH: \int_1^{99} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
- Setting [MATH: a=999,] we have
[MATH: \int_1^{999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
Since the integrals with upper limits [MATH: 99] and [MATH: 999] both give [MATH: 0.171] to [MATH: 3] decimal places, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Some Important Notes

Content:
Before we look at another example, you should note the following important points:

Content:
- In the previous example, you may wonder why we didn't approximate our improper integral by picking a very large value for [MATH: a] right off the bat, e.g.,
[MATH: \int_1^{999\,999\,999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x.]
If we were to try this, one of two things might happen:

- The first is that the calculator might report an error. This is likely due to a lack of physical memory available.
- The second is that the calculator might give an incorrect answer! Evaluating the above on a TI-84 Plus CE-T gives
[MATH: \int_1^{999\,999\,999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 1.348\times 10^{-19}]
which is incorrect! Again, this incorrect answer is likely due to physical limitations that apply to all calculators.

The critical takeaway is that the only safe way to approximate improper integrals is by using the method described earlier.
- In the last example, we increased the upper limit by appending an extra digit [MATH: 9] each time.
[MATH: \int_1^9\qquad \int_1^{99}, \qquad \int_1^{999}, \qquad \int_1^{9\,999}, \qquad \ldots]
If your calculator reports errors before you've reached a definite answer, consider increasing the upper limit more slowly. For example,
[MATH: \int_1^{10}\qquad \int_1^{100}, \qquad \int_1^{200}, \qquad \int_1^{300}, \qquad \ldots\,.]
- Also, bear in mind that some integrals will converge faster than others. Integrals that converge slowly may require us to pick large values for [MATH: a] before we can be sure of our final answer.
- Finally, throughout this lesson, you may assume that all improper integrals we'll encounter are convergent and that all of the functions we'll integrate decay to zero "rapidly enough" for this method to be suitable.
